question: Find the missing number in an array containing n distinct numbers from 0 to n. Most elegant O(1)-space approach?
choices: Sort and binary search
XOR all indices and all values together — the missing number remains
Use a hash set
Sum from 1 to n in a loop
answer: XOR all indices and all values together — the missing number remains
explanation: XOR-ing 0..n with every array value cancels all present numbers (a^a=0), leaving only the missing one. O(n) time, O(1) space.

question: Find All Numbers Disappeared in an Array (values 1..n, some missing) without extra space. What's the trick?
choices: Use a hash set to track seen numbers
Mark visited indices by negating the value at that index
Sort the array first
Use a second array of the same size
answer: Mark visited indices by negating the value at that index
explanation: For each value v, negate the number at index |v|-1. After one pass, positive positions correspond to missing numbers. O(n) time, O(1) extra space.

question: First Missing Positive: find the smallest missing positive integer in O(n) time, O(1) space. What's the key idea?
choices: Sort the array first
Cyclic sort: place each value v at index v-1 if in range, then scan for the first mismatch
Use a hash set of size n
Binary search on the answer
answer: Cyclic sort: place each value v at index v-1 if in range, then scan for the first mismatch
explanation: Swap each valid value into its 'home' index (v at index v-1). Then the first index i where nums[i] != i+1 gives the answer.

question: Set Mismatch: an array 1..n has one number duplicated and one missing. What efficiently finds both?
choices: Sort and scan for the gap
Cyclic sort or sum/sum-of-squares math to solve for both unknowns
Use two hash sets
Binary search twice
answer: Cyclic sort or sum/sum-of-squares math to solve for both unknowns
explanation: Cyclic sort places each number at its correct index in O(n); the index that ends up wrong reveals both the duplicate and the missing value.

question: Reverse a singly linked list iteratively in O(1) space. What three pointers do you track?
choices: head, tail, mid
prev, curr, next
left, right, pivot
slow, fast, prev
answer: prev, curr, next
explanation: Save curr.next before overwriting it, point curr.next to prev, then advance prev and curr forward. Repeat until curr is null.

question: Reverse Linked List II: reverse only the sublist between positions left and right. What's the core technique?
choices: Reverse the entire list then fix the ends
Walk to position left-1, then reverse the sublist in place and reconnect both ends
Copy to an array and rebuild
Use recursion only, no iteration possible
answer: Walk to position left-1, then reverse the sublist in place and reconnect both ends
explanation: Track the node just before the sublist. Reverse nodes between left and right using the standard prev/curr/next pattern, then splice the reversed section back in.

question: Reverse Nodes in k-Group: reverse every k nodes in a linked list. What happens if fewer than k nodes remain at the end?
choices: Reverse them anyway
Leave the remaining nodes as-is (unreversed)
Pad with null nodes
Throw an error
answer: Leave the remaining nodes as-is (unreversed)
explanation: First check if k nodes exist from the current position; if not, stop and leave that final partial group in its original order.

question: Swap Nodes in Pairs: swap every two adjacent nodes in a linked list. What's the pattern for the pointer manipulation?
choices: Swap only the node values
Use a dummy head, then repeatedly relink pairs: prev -> second -> first -> next pair
Reverse the whole list
Convert to array, swap, rebuild
answer: Use a dummy head, then repeatedly relink pairs: prev -> second -> first -> next pair
explanation: A dummy node before the head simplifies edge cases. For each pair, rewire three links so second comes before first, then advance prev to first.

question: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal: return node values grouped by level. What data structure powers this?
choices: Stack
Queue (BFS), processing one full level at a time
Recursion with DFS only
Priority queue
answer: Queue (BFS), processing one full level at a time
explanation: Track the queue size at the start of each level, then dequeue exactly that many nodes before moving to the next level's batch.

question: Binary Tree Zigzag Level Order Traversal alternates left-to-right and right-to-left per level. Simplest way to implement this on top of standard BFS?
choices: Use two separate queues
Standard level-order BFS, then reverse every other level's result list
Use DFS with a visited set
Sort each level's values
answer: Standard level-order BFS, then reverse every other level's result list
explanation: Do normal BFS to collect each level, then reverse the list for every odd-indexed level before appending to the result.

question: Binary Tree Right Side View: return the values visible from the right side. How does BFS solve this cleanly?
choices: Do DFS always going left first
BFS level by level, keep the last node processed in each level
Sort nodes by depth
Use inorder traversal
answer: BFS level by level, keep the last node processed in each level
explanation: The last node dequeued at each level is the rightmost node at that depth — exactly what's visible from the right side.

question: Minimum Depth of Binary Tree (shortest root-to-leaf path). Why is BFS often preferred over DFS here?
choices: BFS uses less memory always
BFS can stop as soon as it finds the first leaf, guaranteeing the shortest path
DFS can't handle trees
BFS is always faster in general
answer: BFS can stop as soon as it finds the first leaf, guaranteeing the shortest path
explanation: BFS explores level by level, so the first leaf encountered is guaranteed to be at minimum depth — no need to explore deeper branches.

question: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree. What's the simplest recursive formula?
choices: depth(root) = depth(root.left) + depth(root.right)
depth(root) = 1 + max(depth(root.left), depth(root.right))
depth(root) = max(root.left, root.right)
depth(root) = count of all nodes
answer: depth(root) = 1 + max(depth(root.left), depth(root.right))
explanation: Each node contributes 1 plus the deeper of its two subtrees. Base case: depth of null is 0.

question: Path Sum: does a root-to-leaf path exist that sums to a target? What's the recursive approach?
choices: BFS level by level summing all nodes
DFS subtracting the current value from target, checking leaves for remaining target == 0
Sort all paths and binary search
Use a hash map of prefix sums
answer: DFS subtracting the current value from target, checking leaves for remaining target == 0
explanation: At each node, recurse into children with target - node.val. A leaf satisfies the condition only if the remaining target equals its own value.

question: Diameter of Binary Tree (longest path between any two nodes). What's the key insight?
choices: It's always root-to-leaf
At each node, diameter through it = left height + right height; track the max globally while computing height
BFS finds it directly
It equals tree depth times 2
answer: At each node, diameter through it = left height + right height; track the max globally while computing height
explanation: A single post-order DFS computes height bottom-up while updating a global max of left height + right height at each node — O(n) instead of recomputing heights repeatedly.

question: Validate Binary Search Tree. Why is 'check left < node < right' for immediate children not sufficient?
choices: It is sufficient
BST validity requires the entire left/right subtree to be within a valid range, not just immediate children
BSTs don't need validation
You only need to check leaves
answer: BST validity requires the entire left/right subtree to be within a valid range, not just immediate children
explanation: Pass down a (min, max) valid range as you recurse. A node deep in the left subtree must still be less than the original root, not just its immediate parent.

question: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum (path can start/end anywhere, not just root-to-leaf). What's the subtlety in the recursion?
choices: Just sum all nodes
Each node returns max single-branch contribution upward, but updates a global max using both branches
Use BFS with level sums
Only consider leaf nodes
answer: Each node returns max single-branch contribution upward, but updates a global max using both branches
explanation: A path through a node can use both children, but a node can only pass ONE branch up to its parent (a valid path can't fork). Track the global max separately, and clip negative branch contributions to 0.

question: IPO / Maximize Capital: pick up to k projects to maximize capital, each project has a cost and profit, you can only afford projects within your capital. What two-heap approach works?
choices: One heap sorted by profit only
Min-heap of costs to find affordable projects, max-heap of profits to greedily pick the best one each round
Sort once and take the first k
Dynamic programming over all subsets
answer: Min-heap of costs to find affordable projects, max-heap of profits to greedily pick the best one each round
explanation: Push all affordable projects (cost <= capital) into a max-heap by profit, pop the best one, add its profit to capital, and repeat k times.

question: Generate all subsets of a set. What's the classic backtracking pattern?
choices: For each element, recurse including it then excluding it, adding the current subset at each call
Only recurse when including elements
Sort the elements first
Use dynamic programming with a 2D table
answer: For each element, recurse including it then excluding it, adding the current subset at each call
explanation: At each index, add the current subset to the result, then recurse forward — the recursion tree naturally explores every include/exclude combination. 2^n subsets total.

question: Subsets II: generate all unique subsets when the input has duplicates. How do you avoid duplicate subsets?
choices: Use a hash set of all subsets to dedupe after generating
Sort first, then skip adjacent duplicate values at the same recursion depth
Remove duplicates from input before starting
It's impossible to avoid duplicates
answer: Sort first, then skip adjacent duplicate values at the same recursion depth
explanation: Sorting groups duplicates together. At each recursive level, skip a value if it equals the previous sibling already tried at that same depth.

question: Generate all permutations of an array. What backtracking pattern is used?
choices: Swap elements in place, recurse, then swap back (undo)
Sort and generate combinations
BFS level by level
Use a hash map of counts
answer: Swap elements in place, recurse, then swap back (undo)
explanation: Fix each position by swapping in every remaining candidate, recurse to fill the rest, then swap back to restore state for the next candidate — the 'choose, explore, unchoose' pattern.

question: Combination Sum: find all combinations that sum to a target, reusing numbers freely. Why does the recursion stay at the same index when a number is used?
choices: To avoid stack overflow
Because numbers can be reused unlimited times, so you don't advance past the current candidate
It's a bug in the standard solution
To guarantee sorted output
answer: Because numbers can be reused unlimited times, so you don't advance past the current candidate
explanation: Since the same number can be picked multiple times, recursing with the same start index (not index+1) allows reuse, while still moving forward to i+1 for numbers you choose not to use.

question: Generate Parentheses: produce all valid combinations of n pairs of parentheses. What two counters guide the backtracking?
choices: Total length only
Count of open parens used and count of close parens used, with close <= open <= n
Depth of recursion only
Number of valid strings found so far
answer: Count of open parens used and count of close parens used, with close <= open <= n
explanation: Add '(' whenever open < n, add ')' whenever close < open — this constraint ensures every prefix is valid, avoiding invalid branches entirely.

question: Palindrome Partitioning: partition a string into all possible palindromic substrings. What's the backtracking structure?
choices: Try every substring starting at the current index; recurse on the remainder only if the prefix is a palindrome
Use dynamic programming exclusively, no recursion
Sort characters first
Only check the whole string at once
answer: Try every substring starting at the current index; recurse on the remainder only if the prefix is a palindrome
explanation: At each position, try all possible end points for the next palindrome piece, recursing on the rest of the string only when the current piece is itself a palindrome.

question: N-Queens: place N queens so none attack each other. What sets does backtracking track to check attacks in O(1)?
choices: Only a 2D board array, checked cell by cell
Sets for used columns, and two sets for diagonals (row-col and row+col)
A single hash set of all positions
Sort queens by row only
answer: Sets for used columns, and two sets for diagonals (row-col and row+col)
explanation: row-col is constant along a '\' diagonal, row+col is constant along a '/' diagonal. Tracking columns and both diagonal sets lets you validate placement in O(1) instead of scanning the board.

question: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array. How do you decide which half to search?
choices: Always go left
Compare mid to the right boundary: if nums[mid] > nums[right], min is in the right half, else left half (including mid)
Linear scan is required
Compare mid to the first element only
answer: Compare mid to the right boundary: if nums[mid] > nums[right], min is in the right half, else left half (including mid)
explanation: If nums[mid] > nums[right], the rotation point (minimum) is to the right of mid. Otherwise, the left portion including mid may contain the minimum.

question: Search a 2D Matrix where rows and columns are sorted. What's an O(log(m*n)) approach?
choices: Search each row with linear scan
Treat the matrix as a flattened sorted array and binary search using index math (row = idx/n, col = idx%n)
Search from the top-right corner only
Use DFS
answer: Treat the matrix as a flattened sorted array and binary search using index math (row = idx/n, col = idx%n)
explanation: If each row starts where the previous ends, the whole matrix is effectively one sorted array — mid index converts to (mid/cols, mid%cols).

question: Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array. How do you get O(log n) for both bounds?
choices: One binary search, then scan left and right linearly
Two separate binary searches: one biased to find the leftmost match, one biased to find the rightmost
Sort again and use indexOf
Use a hash map of positions
answer: Two separate binary searches: one biased to find the leftmost match, one biased to find the rightmost
explanation: Run binary search that keeps narrowing right even after finding a match (for leftmost), and a mirrored version keeping narrowing left (for rightmost). Both are O(log n).

question: Koko Eating Bananas: find the minimum eating speed to finish all bananas within h hours. Why is this 'binary search on the answer'?
choices: Because the bananas are sorted
The feasibility of a speed is monotonic — if speed k works, any faster speed also works, so you binary search over possible speeds
It's actually a greedy problem, not binary search
Because h is always a power of two
answer: The feasibility of a speed is monotonic — if speed k works, any faster speed also works, so you binary search over possible speeds
explanation: Binary search over the answer space (1 to max pile) works whenever 'can we succeed with value X' is monotonic — a very common pattern for optimization problems disguised as search problems.

question: Search in Rotated Sorted Array II allows duplicates. Why does this break the O(log n) guarantee of the no-duplicate version?
choices: It doesn't break anything
When nums[left] == nums[mid] == nums[right], you can't tell which half is sorted, forcing a linear step (shrink both ends by 1)
Duplicates make binary search impossible entirely
You need a hash map instead
answer: When nums[left] == nums[mid] == nums[right], you can't tell which half is sorted, forcing a linear step (shrink both ends by 1)
explanation: With duplicates, the usual 'one half is always sorted' trick can become ambiguous. The fallback of shrinking both pointers by one degrades worst case to O(n).

question: Top K Frequent Words: return the k most frequent words, ties broken alphabetically. What heap comparator handles both rules?
choices: Compare by frequency only
Min-heap of size k comparing by (frequency ascending, then word descending) so the 'worst' item is always poppable
Max-heap of all words, pop k times
Sort alphabetically first, ignore frequency
answer: Min-heap of size k comparing by (frequency ascending, then word descending) so the 'worst' item is always poppable
explanation: A size-k min-heap keeps only the best k candidates seen so far; the custom comparator (lower freq, or same freq but lexicographically larger) identifies which item to evict when a better one arrives.

question: K Closest Points to Origin. Why is a max-heap of size k often better than sorting all points?
choices: Max-heap is always faster in every case
Sorting is O(n log n); a size-k max-heap keeping the k closest is O(n log k), better when k << n
Max-heap uses less memory always
Sorting can't handle 2D points
answer: Sorting is O(n log n); a size-k max-heap keeping the k closest is O(n log k), better when k << n
explanation: Push points onto a max-heap by distance, popping the farthest whenever size exceeds k. This keeps the heap small and avoids sorting the entire input.

question: Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix (rows and columns sorted). What's an efficient heap-based approach?
choices: Flatten and sort the whole matrix
Min-heap seeded with the first column/row, popping smallest and pushing its right/down neighbor k times
Binary search on matrix values only
DFS from the top-left corner
answer: Min-heap seeded with the first column/row, popping smallest and pushing its right/down neighbor k times
explanation: This is a k-way merge in disguise: each row is a sorted list. Seed the heap with the first element of each row, then pop-and-push k times to reach the kth smallest.

question: Sort Characters By Frequency: rebuild a string with characters ordered by descending frequency. What's the standard approach?
choices: Sort characters alphabetically
Count frequencies with a hash map, then sort or heap-order by count descending
Use a trie
Reverse the string
answer: Count frequencies with a hash map, then sort or heap-order by count descending
explanation: Build a frequency map in O(n), then either sort entries by count (O(n log n)) or use bucket sort by frequency for O(n) since frequency is bounded by string length.

question: Merge K Sorted Lists. What's the most efficient standard approach?
choices: Merge them one at a time sequentially — O(k²n)
Min-heap holding the current head of each list, repeatedly popping the smallest and pushing its next node
Concatenate all and sort — O(kn log(kn))
Use a single pointer walking all lists simultaneously
answer: Min-heap holding the current head of each list, repeatedly popping the smallest and pushing its next node
explanation: A heap of size k always exposes the global smallest current head in O(log k) per operation, giving O(n log k) total — better than sequential merging or full sort.

question: Kth Smallest Element in a sorted matrix / m sorted lists — what generalizes 'merge 2 sorted lists' to k lists efficiently?
choices: Repeated pairwise merging is the only option
A min-heap based k-way merge, which is the generalization of the two-pointer merge used for 2 lists
Binary search alone, no merging needed
Bubble sort across all lists
answer: A min-heap based k-way merge, which is the generalization of the two-pointer merge used for 2 lists
explanation: Two-pointer merge (2 lists) generalizes to a heap holding one pointer per list — the heap replaces manually comparing k pointers each step.

question: Smallest Range Covering Elements from K Lists. Why is a min-heap the right structure here too?
choices: It sorts the final answer
The heap always tracks the current minimum across all k lists while you track the current maximum separately, shrinking the range as you advance
It avoids needing k pointers
It reduces space to O(1)
answer: The heap always tracks the current minimum across all k lists while you track the current maximum separately, shrinking the range as you advance
explanation: Pop the current min from the heap (this bounds the range's left edge), push the next element from that same list, and track the max seen so far as the range's right edge — repeat until any list is exhausted.

question: Course Schedule II: return a valid course order given prerequisites (or empty if impossible). What algorithm and structure?
choices: DFS returning nodes in any visited order
Kahn's algorithm: BFS using in-degree counts, processing nodes with in-degree 0 first
Sort courses numerically
Union-Find only
answer: Kahn's algorithm: BFS using in-degree counts, processing nodes with in-degree 0 first
explanation: Compute in-degree for every node, queue all in-degree-0 nodes, then repeatedly dequeue, add to result, and decrement neighbors' in-degree, queueing any that hit 0. If not all nodes get processed, a cycle exists.

question: Alien Dictionary: derive character ordering from a sorted list of words in an alien language. Where do the graph edges come from?
choices: Compare every pair of characters in every word
Compare adjacent words character by character; the first differing character pair gives an ordering edge
Count character frequency
Sort characters alphabetically as a baseline
answer: Compare adjacent words character by character; the first differing character pair gives an ordering edge
explanation: For each pair of adjacent words, find the first position where characters differ — that gives one 'comes before' edge. Then topologically sort the resulting character graph.

question: Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph. Why is Union-Find a natural fit?
choices: It requires sorting edges first
Each union operation merges components; the final count of distinct roots is the answer, all in near O(1) per operation with path compression
It's the only way to solve it
DFS can't solve this problem
answer: Each union operation merges components; the final count of distinct roots is the answer, all in near O(1) per operation with path compression
explanation: Start with n components. For each edge, union the two nodes; if they were already connected, the component count doesn't decrease. DFS/BFS also works, but Union-Find is often simpler for streaming edges.

question: Redundant Connection: find the edge that creates a cycle in a graph that was originally a tree. What does Union-Find detect?
choices: The edge with the highest weight
The edge connecting two nodes that are already in the same component
The first edge added
The node with the most connections
answer: The edge connecting two nodes that are already in the same component
explanation: Process edges in order, union-ing endpoints. The moment an edge connects two nodes that already share a root, that edge is the redundant one creating the cycle.

question: Accounts Merge: merge accounts that share any email. Why is Union-Find preferred over building a full graph and DFS?
choices: DFS can't handle strings
Union-Find handles merging groups incrementally and efficiently as shared emails are discovered, with near-constant time per union
It's not preferred; DFS is always better
Union-Find sorts emails automatically
answer: Union-Find handles merging groups incrementally and efficiently as shared emails are discovered, with near-constant time per union
explanation: Union each account index with every other account sharing an email. Path compression and union by rank make this close to O(1) per operation, then group final results by root.

question: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree) with insert/search/startsWith. What's the core structure of each node?
choices: An array of 26 booleans only
A map/array of child nodes (one per character) plus an 'end of word' flag
A single string field
A hash set of all words
answer: A map/array of child nodes (one per character) plus an 'end of word' flag
explanation: Each node holds pointers to its children (indexed by character) and a boolean marking whether a complete word ends there. Insert/search walk character by character, O(word length) each.

question: Word Search II: find all dictionary words present in a 2D board. Why combine a Trie with DFS instead of searching each word separately?
choices: Trie makes DFS unnecessary
The Trie lets DFS explore all words sharing a prefix simultaneously, pruning paths that match no word early
It's purely for memory savings
Tries only work with sorted words
answer: The Trie lets DFS explore all words sharing a prefix simultaneously, pruning paths that match no word early
explanation: Insert all words into a Trie, then DFS from each board cell following Trie edges — if no Trie child matches, prune immediately instead of continuing a doomed path. Much faster than running Word Search per word.

question: Single Number: every element appears twice except one. Find it in O(1) space. What's the trick?
choices: Use a hash set to track seen numbers
XOR all numbers together — pairs cancel out (a^a=0), leaving the single number
Sort and scan for the break
Sum all numbers and divide
answer: XOR all numbers together — pairs cancel out (a^a=0), leaving the single number
explanation: XOR is commutative and associative, and a^a=0, a^0=a. XOR-ing the whole array cancels every pair, leaving only the unpaired value. O(n) time, O(1) space.

question: Single Number II: every element appears three times except one. Why doesn't simple XOR work here?
choices: XOR only works for even counts of duplicates — three copies don't cancel to zero
It does work, just apply XOR three times
Because negative numbers break XOR
Because the array must be sorted first
answer: XOR only works for even counts of duplicates — three copies don't cancel to zero
explanation: With triples, you need bit counting: sum each bit position across all numbers mod 3; any bit that remains set belongs to the single number. Sometimes solved with two bitmasks tracking 'seen once' and 'seen twice'.

question: Counting Bits: for every number 0..n, count the number of 1 bits, in O(n) total time. What's the DP recurrence?
choices: bits[i] = bits[i-1] + 1
bits[i] = bits[i >> 1] + (i & 1)
bits[i] = i % 2
bits[i] = log2(i)
answer: bits[i] = bits[i >> 1] + (i & 1)
explanation: Right-shifting i by 1 removes the last bit; bits[i] equals the bit count of i>>1 plus whether the last bit (i&1) is set — reuses previously computed answers instead of counting bits from scratch each time.

question: Add two integers without using the + or - operator. What bitwise operations simulate addition?
choices: Multiplication and division only
XOR for sum without carry, AND shifted left by 1 for carry, repeat until carry is zero
OR and NOT only
Convert to strings and concatenate
answer: XOR for sum without carry, AND shifted left by 1 for carry, repeat until carry is zero
explanation: a^b gives sum ignoring carry; (a&b)<<1 gives the carry bits. Repeatedly apply until there's no carry left — this is literally how hardware adders work.

question: Climbing Stairs: count ways to reach step n taking 1 or 2 steps at a time. What's the recurrence?
choices: dp[n] = dp[n-1] * dp[n-2]
dp[n] = dp[n-1] + dp[n-2]
dp[n] = dp[n-1] - dp[n-2]
dp[n] = max(dp[n-1], dp[n-2])
answer: dp[n] = dp[n-1] + dp[n-2]
explanation: To reach step n, your last move was either from n-1 (1 step) or n-2 (2 steps) — this is literally the Fibonacci recurrence.

question: Partition Equal Subset Sum: can the array be split into two subsets with equal sum? What DP pattern does this reduce to?
choices: Longest increasing subsequence
0/1 Knapsack: does a subset sum to exactly total/2?
Unbounded knapsack
Greedy interval scheduling
answer: 0/1 Knapsack: does a subset sum to exactly total/2?
explanation: If total sum is odd, it's impossible. Otherwise it's exactly the 0/1 knapsack question 'can some subset reach target = total/2', solved with a boolean DP array.

question: Target Sum: assign +/- signs to array elements to reach a target. Why is this also a 0/1 knapsack problem?
choices: It isn't related to knapsack at all
It reduces to finding a subset P with sum (target+total)/2, since P - N = target and P + N = total
It's solved with BFS only
It requires sorting the array first
answer: It reduces to finding a subset P with sum (target+total)/2, since P - N = target and P + N = total
explanation: Let P be the positive-sign subset sum and N the negative one. Solving the two equations gives P = (target + total)/2 — now it's 'count subsets summing to P', classic knapsack DP.

question: Coin Change II: count the number of ways to make an amount (order doesn't matter). Why must coins be the outer loop, not the inner loop?
choices: It doesn't matter which loop is outer
Coins outer + amount inner avoids counting permutations of the same combination as distinct ways
Amount must always be outer for correctness
Because coins need to be sorted first
answer: Coins outer + amount inner avoids counting permutations of the same combination as distinct ways
explanation: Looping coins on the outside ensures each coin type is fully 'decided' before moving to the next, counting combinations. Swapping loop order would count [1,2] and [2,1] as different ways — permutations, not combinations.

question: Longest Common Subsequence between two strings. What's the DP recurrence?
choices: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 always
If chars match: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1; else dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])
dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]) always
dp[i][j] = min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])
answer: If chars match: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1; else dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])
explanation: Matching characters extend the diagonal subsequence by 1; otherwise you take the best result from dropping a character off either string.

question: Edit Distance (min operations to convert one string to another). What three operations does each DP cell consider?
choices: Insert, delete, substitute
Swap, reverse, delete
Insert, reverse, substitute
Only substitute is allowed
answer: Insert, delete, substitute
explanation: dp[i][j] = min(dp[i-1][j]+1 [delete], dp[i][j-1]+1 [insert], dp[i-1][j-1]+cost [substitute, cost=0 if chars match else 1]).

question: Longest Palindromic Substring. What's a common O(n²) approach that avoids full DP tables?
choices: Sort the string
Expand around each center (both odd and even length centers)
Reverse the string and use LCS
Use a hash map of substrings
answer: Expand around each center (both odd and even length centers)
explanation: For each index (and each gap between indices for even-length palindromes), expand outward while characters match. O(n²) time, O(1) space — simpler than a full DP table.

question: Longest Palindromic Subsequence. How does this differ from Longest Palindromic Substring in approach?
choices: It's identical, just call LCS with no changes
It's the LCS of the string and its reverse
It requires backtracking, not DP
It can be solved with a single pass, no table
answer: It's the LCS of the string and its reverse
explanation: A palindromic subsequence read forwards equals itself read backwards, so LPS(s) = LCS(s, reverse(s)) — a neat reduction to a problem you already know.

question: Unique Paths in an m x n grid (only right/down moves). What's the DP recurrence?
choices: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] * dp[i][j-1]
dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1]
dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])
answer: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1]
explanation: Any cell can only be reached from above or from the left, so the number of ways to reach it is the sum of ways to reach those two neighbors. First row/column are all 1.

question: Decode Ways: count ways to decode a digit string into letters (A=1..Z=26). What makes a two-digit group valid to decode together?
choices: Any two digits
The two-digit number formed is between 10 and 26
The digits must be equal
Only if the first digit is 1
answer: The two-digit number formed is between 10 and 26
explanation: dp[i] = dp[i-1] (if current digit is 1-9) + dp[i-2] (if the two-digit number s[i-2:i] is between 10 and 26) — similar shape to climbing stairs with validity checks.

question: Jump Game: can you reach the last index given max jump lengths at each position? What's the O(n) greedy approach?
choices: Try every combination of jumps (backtracking)
Track the farthest reachable index while scanning left to right; if you reach it before it stalls, you can finish
Always jump the maximum distance
Use dynamic programming with O(n²) time
answer: Track the farthest reachable index while scanning left to right; if you reach it before it stalls, you can finish
explanation: Maintain farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i]) as you scan. If at any index i > farthest, you're stuck. If farthest reaches the last index, you can finish.

question: Jump Game II: find the minimum number of jumps to reach the end. What greedy pattern minimizes jumps?
choices: Always jump the farthest single step available
BFS-like leveling: track the current jump's boundary and the farthest reachable in the next jump; increment jumps when you cross the boundary
Dynamic programming is the only option
Random jumping
answer: BFS-like leveling: track the current jump's boundary and the farthest reachable in the next jump; increment jumps when you cross the boundary
explanation: This is essentially BFS by levels without a queue: each 'jump' is a level. When you reach the current level's boundary, you must have already jumped, so increment count and update the new boundary.

question: Gas Station: find the starting index to complete a circular route, given gas and cost arrays. What's the greedy insight?
choices: Try every starting point and simulate — O(n²)
If total gas >= total cost a solution exists; the start is right after the point where cumulative tank first goes negative
Sort stations by gas amount
Use dynamic programming over all subsets
answer: If total gas >= total cost a solution exists; the start is right after the point where cumulative tank first goes negative
explanation: If the total gas is enough overall, exactly one valid start exists. Track a running tank total; whenever it goes negative, no station in that stretch could be the start, so reset the candidate start to the next index.

question: Daily Temperatures: for each day, find how many days until a warmer temperature. What stack pattern solves this in O(n)?
choices: Sort temperatures and compare
Monotonic decreasing stack of indices; pop and compute distance whenever a warmer day is found
Use nested loops checking every future day
Binary search on temperature values
answer: Monotonic decreasing stack of indices; pop and compute distance whenever a warmer day is found
explanation: Push indices while temperatures are non-increasing. When a warmer day appears, pop all indices with lower temps and record the distance — each index is pushed/popped once, giving O(n).

question: Next Greater Element I: for each element, find the next greater element to its right. What's the efficient pattern?
choices: Nested loop checking all following elements — O(n²)
Monotonic decreasing stack processed once, mapping each element to its next greater via a hash map
Sort the array and binary search
Use two pointers from both ends
answer: Monotonic decreasing stack processed once, mapping each element to its next greater via a hash map
explanation: Scan once, maintaining a stack of elements awaiting their 'next greater'. Whenever the current element is bigger than the stack top, pop and record the current element as its answer.

question: Largest Rectangle in Histogram. What does the monotonic increasing stack store, and when do you pop?
choices: It stores heights only, popping never
It stores indices of increasing bar heights; pop and compute area whenever a shorter bar appears
It stores all rectangles found so far
It's solved with a heap, not a stack
answer: It stores indices of increasing bar heights; pop and compute area whenever a shorter bar appears
explanation: When a shorter bar appears, the popped bar's rectangle can't extend further right, so compute its area using width = current index - new stack top index - 1.

question: Online Stock Span: for a stream of prices, find how many consecutive prior days had price <= today's. What's the pattern?
choices: Recompute the span from scratch every day — O(n²)
Monotonic decreasing stack of (price, span) pairs; pop and accumulate spans while stack top's price <= today's
Sort all prices seen so far
Use a hash map of price to day
answer: Monotonic decreasing stack of (price, span) pairs; pop and accumulate spans while stack top's price <= today's
explanation: Pop every day whose price is less than or equal to today's, absorbing their spans into today's span before pushing — amortized O(1) per query.

question: Range Sum Query - Immutable: answer many sum(i,j) queries efficiently on a static array. What preprocessing helps?
choices: Sort the array
Build a prefix sum array once: sum(i,j) = prefix[j+1] - prefix[i]
Use a hash map of all possible ranges
Recompute the sum for each query
answer: Build a prefix sum array once: sum(i,j) = prefix[j+1] - prefix[i]
explanation: O(n) preprocessing turns every subsequent range-sum query into O(1) instead of O(n) per query — huge win when there are many queries.

question: Continuous Subarray Sum: does a subarray of length >= 2 sum to a multiple of k? What prefix sum trick applies?
choices: Check every pair of indices directly — O(n²)
Track prefix sum mod k in a hash map; if the same remainder appears at two indices >= 2 apart, that subarray sums to a multiple of k
Sort the array first
Use a sliding window only
answer: Track prefix sum mod k in a hash map; if the same remainder appears at two indices >= 2 apart, that subarray sums to a multiple of k
explanation: If prefixSum[i] % k == prefixSum[j] % k, the subarray between i and j sums to a multiple of k (their difference removes whole multiples of k). Store the first index each remainder is seen.

question: Word Ladder: find the shortest transformation sequence length between two words, changing one letter at a time. Why BFS, not DFS?
choices: DFS is actually preferred
BFS explores level by level, guaranteeing the first time you reach the end word is via the shortest path
Word Ladder can't be modeled as a graph
BFS uses less memory in every case
answer: BFS explores level by level, guaranteeing the first time you reach the end word is via the shortest path
explanation: Each word is a node; edges connect words differing by one letter. BFS from the start word guarantees the shortest path length is found the moment the end word is dequeued.

question: Network Delay Time: find the time for a signal to reach all nodes from a source, given weighted directed edges. What algorithm fits?
choices: BFS, since it's a graph problem
Dijkstra's algorithm, since all edge weights are non-negative and you need shortest paths from one source
DFS with backtracking
Union-Find
answer: Dijkstra's algorithm, since all edge weights are non-negative and you need shortest paths from one source
explanation: A min-heap of (distance, node) pairs greedily expands the closest unvisited node each step — classic single-source shortest path for non-negative weighted graphs.

question: Number of Provinces: count connected groups of cities given an adjacency matrix. What's a simple approach?
choices: Sort the matrix
DFS or BFS from each unvisited city, counting how many traversals are needed to cover all cities
Binary search on the matrix
Only Union-Find works
answer: DFS or BFS from each unvisited city, counting how many traversals are needed to cover all cities
explanation: For each unvisited city, run DFS/BFS to mark its whole connected component, incrementing a province counter each time you start a new traversal.

question: Rotting Oranges: find the minimum time for all fresh oranges to rot, given rotten ones spread to adjacent cells each minute. What's the pattern?
choices: DFS from each rotten orange independently
Multi-source BFS: start with all rotten oranges in the queue simultaneously, processing level by level (each level = 1 minute)
Sort oranges by position
Dynamic programming over grid cells
answer: Multi-source BFS: start with all rotten oranges in the queue simultaneously, processing level by level (each level = 1 minute)
explanation: Seed the BFS queue with every initially rotten orange at once (not just one). Each BFS 'layer' represents exactly one minute passing, which naturally gives the minimum time.

question: Design an LRU Cache with O(1) get and put. What two structures work together?
choices: A single array with linear search
Hash map (key -> node) combined with a doubly linked list tracking recency order
A sorted array with binary search
A single hash map only
answer: Hash map (key -> node) combined with a doubly linked list tracking recency order
explanation: The hash map gives O(1) lookup to a node; the doubly linked list lets you move that node to the front (most recent) and evict from the back (least recent) in O(1), since you can unlink a node without scanning.

question: Min Stack: design a stack supporting push, pop, top, and getMin all in O(1). What's the trick?
choices: Sort the stack after every push
Maintain a second stack that tracks the minimum at each level alongside the main stack
Scan the whole stack for getMin
Use a heap instead of a stack
answer: Maintain a second stack that tracks the minimum at each level alongside the main stack
explanation: Push the current minimum (min of new value and previous min) onto an auxiliary stack in lockstep with the main stack, so getMin is just peeking the aux stack — O(1).

question: Implement a Queue using two Stacks. What's the amortized cost per operation?
choices: O(n) for every operation
O(1) amortized — elements move from the 'in' stack to the 'out' stack only when the out stack is empty
O(log n) using a heap internally
It's impossible with just two stacks
answer: O(1) amortized — elements move from the 'in' stack to the 'out' stack only when the out stack is empty
explanation: Push always goes to the 'in' stack. Dequeue pops from 'out'; if 'out' is empty, dump all of 'in' into 'out' (reversing order), which happens rarely enough that the amortized cost per operation is O(1).

question: Design an LFU Cache (evict least frequently used, ties broken by least recently used). What structure tracks frequency groups efficiently?
choices: A single hash map of key to value
Hash map of key->node plus hash map of frequency->doubly linked list of nodes at that frequency, tracking min frequency
A sorted array of all entries
A max-heap of frequencies only
answer: Hash map of key->node plus hash map of frequency->doubly linked list of nodes at that frequency, tracking min frequency
explanation: Each frequency bucket is its own LRU list (recency breaks ties). A tracked 'min frequency' pointer lets eviction go straight to the right bucket in O(1) instead of scanning for the least-frequent key.

question: Rotate Image (rotate an n x n matrix 90 degrees in place). What two-step transformation achieves this in O(1) extra space?
choices: Reverse rows only
Transpose the matrix, then reverse each row
Reverse columns, then transpose
Sort each row
answer: Transpose the matrix, then reverse each row
explanation: Transposing (swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i]) followed by reversing each row produces exactly a 90-degree clockwise rotation, all without allocating a new matrix.

question: Spiral Matrix: return all elements in spiral order. What's the standard boundary-tracking approach?
choices: Recursively peel one ring at a time is not possible
Track four boundaries (top, bottom, left, right) and shrink them inward after traversing each side
Use DFS from the center outward
Sort elements by distance from center
answer: Track four boundaries (top, bottom, left, right) and shrink them inward after traversing each side
explanation: Traverse right across the top row, down the right column, left across the bottom row, up the left column, shrinking each boundary after its pass, until boundaries cross.

question: Set Matrix Zeroes: if an element is 0, set its entire row and column to 0, using O(1) extra space. What's the trick?
choices: Use a separate boolean matrix to track zeros
Use the first row and first column of the matrix itself as marker flags, with separate flags for whether the first row/col themselves need zeroing
Copy the whole matrix first
It's impossible in O(1) space
answer: Use the first row and first column of the matrix itself as marker flags, with separate flags for whether the first row/col themselves need zeroing
explanation: Instead of extra memory, repurpose the first row/column as a marker array: matrix[i][0]=0 means row i should be zeroed, matrix[0][j]=0 means column j should be. Track the first row/col's own zero status with two separate booleans.

question: You need frequent random access by index and rarely insert/delete except at the end. Array or Linked List?
choices: Array
Linked List
Both are identical in performance
Neither, use a hash map
answer: Array
explanation: Array: O(1) random access via memory offset, but O(n) insert/delete in the middle. Linked List: O(1) insert/delete once you have a pointer, but O(n) to reach an index. Pick based on your dominant operation.

question: You're inserting and deleting at both ends frequently (e.g. implementing a sliding window). Array-based List or Deque?
choices: Array-based List (like Python list / Java ArrayList)
Deque (double-ended queue, e.g. collections.deque)
Singly Linked List
Hash Set
answer: Deque (double-ended queue, e.g. collections.deque)
explanation: A deque (usually backed by a doubly linked list or a circular buffer) gives O(1) push/pop at both ends. A plain array-based list is O(1) at the end but O(n) at the front, since every element must shift.

question: You need LIFO order (most recent thing processed first) — e.g. matching parentheses or undo history. Stack or Queue?
choices: Stack
Queue
They're interchangeable
Priority Queue
answer: Stack
explanation: Stack is Last-In-First-Out: push/pop from the same end. Queue is First-In-First-Out. Use a stack whenever you need to 'undo' or match the most recent unmatched item — brackets, DFS, backtracking, call stacks.

question: You need FIFO order (process things in the order they arrived) — e.g. BFS traversal or a task queue. Stack or Queue?
choices: Stack
Queue
Heap
Trie
answer: Queue
explanation: Queue processes First-In-First-Out. This is exactly why BFS uses a queue (explore nodes in the order discovered) while DFS uses a stack (explore the most recently discovered node first).

question: You need O(1) average lookup/insert by key and don't care about ordering. Hash Map or Balanced BST (TreeMap)?
choices: Hash Map
Balanced BST (TreeMap/TreeSet)
Array with binary search
Linked List
answer: Hash Map
explanation: Hash Map gives O(1) average time for get/put via hashing, but no ordering guarantee. Use a TreeMap only when you need sorted iteration, range queries, or floor/ceiling operations — those cost O(log n) but stay ordered.

question: You need to repeatedly find the min or max, and the set of elements changes often. Heap or sort the array each time?
choices: Sort the array on every change
Heap (priority queue)
Hash Set
Linked List
answer: Heap (priority queue)
explanation: A heap gives O(log n) insert and O(log n) remove-min/max, and O(1) peek. Re-sorting after every change costs O(n log n) each time — a heap amortizes far better when there are many updates.

question: You need the Kth largest element only once, not a live priority queue. Full sort, or heap, or quickselect?
choices: Full sort: O(n log n)
Heap of size k: O(n log k)
Quickselect: O(n) average
All are equally good, pick any
answer: Quickselect: O(n) average
explanation: If you need a one-time answer (not a running structure), quickselect's average O(n) beats both full sort O(n log n) and heap O(n log k). But quickselect has O(n²) worst case and doesn't preserve order — a heap is preferable if you need the full top-k list or must stream updates.

question: You need to check if a string exists in a large dictionary, plus autocomplete by prefix. HashSet or Trie?
choices: HashSet — O(1) average lookup is always enough
Trie — enables efficient prefix queries that a HashSet can't do directly
Sorted array with binary search
Linked List of all words
answer: Trie — enables efficient prefix queries that a HashSet can't do directly
explanation: HashSet gives O(1) exact-match lookup but can't efficiently answer 'find all words starting with X' — you'd have to scan every entry. A Trie walks character by character, making prefix search O(prefix length), independent of dictionary size.

question: Your graph is sparse (few edges relative to nodes, e.g. a social network). Adjacency List or Adjacency Matrix?
choices: Adjacency List
Adjacency Matrix
Both use the same space
Neither works for sparse graphs
answer: Adjacency List
explanation: Adjacency List uses O(V+E) space — efficient for sparse graphs. Adjacency Matrix always uses O(V²) space regardless of edge count, which wastes memory when E << V². Matrix wins only when you need O(1) edge-existence checks on a dense graph.

question: You need to check whether an edge exists between two specific nodes in O(1) time, and the graph is small/dense. Adjacency List or Matrix?
choices: Adjacency List — O(degree) to check
Adjacency Matrix — O(1) direct lookup
Neither supports this
Union-Find only
answer: Adjacency Matrix — O(1) direct lookup
explanation: matrix[u][v] is a direct O(1) check. An adjacency list requires scanning u's neighbor list, O(degree(u)). The tradeoff is O(V²) space for the matrix vs O(V+E) for the list.

question: You need to explore as deep as possible before backtracking (e.g. maze solving, topological sort, cycle detection). DFS or BFS?
choices: DFS
BFS
Either works identically
Dijkstra's algorithm
answer: DFS
explanation: DFS naturally fits problems needing full-path exploration, backtracking, or ordering constraints (topological sort). BFS is the better fit when you need the shortest path in an unweighted graph, since it explores in layers of increasing distance.

question: You need the shortest path between two nodes in an unweighted graph. DFS or BFS?
choices: DFS
BFS
Either works identically
You need Dijkstra's algorithm
answer: BFS
explanation: BFS explores nodes in order of distance from the source, so the first time you reach the target, that path is guaranteed shortest. DFS can find *a* path but not necessarily the shortest one.

question: You need shortest paths in a graph with weighted, non-negative edges. BFS or Dijkstra's algorithm?
choices: BFS
Dijkstra's algorithm (min-heap based)
DFS
Union-Find
answer: Dijkstra's algorithm (min-heap based)
explanation: BFS assumes all edges have equal weight (1), so it only gives correct shortest paths on unweighted graphs. Dijkstra's uses a min-heap to always expand the currently-closest node, correctly handling varying edge weights — as long as no edge is negative.

question: Your weighted graph may contain negative edge weights. Dijkstra's algorithm or Bellman-Ford?
choices: Dijkstra's algorithm
Bellman-Ford
Either works the same
BFS
answer: Bellman-Ford
explanation: Dijkstra's greedy 'never revisit a finalized node' assumption breaks with negative edges — a later negative edge could improve an already-finalized shortest path. Bellman-Ford relaxes all edges V-1 times and can even detect negative cycles, at the cost of O(V*E) vs Dijkstra's O(E log V).

question: You need to detect a cycle or check connectivity in an undirected graph with edges arriving one at a time (e.g. Kruskal's MST). Union-Find or DFS?
choices: DFS — must rebuild the visited set from scratch each time
Union-Find — incrementally tracks components with near O(1) amortized union/find
Neither can handle streaming edges
BFS only
answer: Union-Find — incrementally tracks components with near O(1) amortized union/find
explanation: DFS works but requires re-traversing the whole graph to re-check connectivity after each new edge. Union-Find (with path compression + union by rank) updates and queries connectivity incrementally in near-constant amortized time per operation.

question: A problem asks for the *optimal value* and has overlapping subproblems where local greedy choices can be wrong (e.g. 0/1 Knapsack). Greedy or Dynamic Programming?
choices: Greedy — always pick the locally best option
Dynamic Programming — explore all valid choices, reusing overlapping subproblem results
Backtracking without memoization
Sorting alone
answer: Dynamic Programming — explore all valid choices, reusing overlapping subproblem results
explanation: Greedy works only when a problem has the 'greedy choice property' (local optimum leads to global optimum), like activity selection or Huffman coding. When that property doesn't hold (0/1 Knapsack, Longest Common Subsequence), you need DP to consider all valid combinations.

question: A problem has the greedy choice property AND optimal substructure (e.g. interval scheduling, Dijkstra's, Huffman coding). Greedy or DP?
choices: Greedy — simpler and often faster, O(n log n) vs DP's higher complexity
DP is always safer, use it regardless
Backtracking is required
Neither applies
answer: Greedy — simpler and often faster, O(n log n) vs DP's higher complexity
explanation: When making the locally optimal choice at each step is provably part of some globally optimal solution, greedy is both simpler and asymptotically faster than DP — but you must prove the greedy property holds, or you'll get wrong answers on some inputs.

question: You're implementing DP and want to avoid computing subproblems you'll never actually need. Top-down memoization or bottom-up tabulation?
choices: Top-down memoization (recursion + cache)
Bottom-up tabulation (iterative table filling)
Both compute the exact same subproblems always
Neither approach matters for efficiency
answer: Top-down memoization (recursion + cache)
explanation: Memoization only computes subproblems actually reached by the recursion, which can save work when many states are unreachable. Tabulation computes every state in a fixed order, which is often faster in practice (no recursion overhead) and easier to optimize for space, but always fills the whole table.

question: You're worried about stack overflow on deep recursive DFS over a huge tree/graph. Recursion or an explicit iterative stack?
choices: Recursion — the call stack handles everything automatically
Explicit iterative stack — avoids relying on the language's call stack depth limit
Neither matters, depth is never an issue
Use a queue instead of a stack
answer: Explicit iterative stack — avoids relying on the language's call stack depth limit
explanation: Recursive DFS is cleaner to write, but each call frame consumes call-stack memory; a sufficiently deep/unbalanced tree can trigger a stack overflow. Converting to an explicit stack-based loop removes that limit (bounded only by heap memory).

question: You need to find a contiguous subarray/substring satisfying some condition, and the window boundaries move monotonically forward. Sliding Window or Two Pointers from both ends?
choices: Sliding Window (both pointers move forward, window expands/contracts)
Two Pointers converging from opposite ends
Neither applies, use brute force
Binary search on the window size only
answer: Sliding Window (both pointers move forward, window expands/contracts)
explanation: Sliding window is really a specialized two-pointer technique for *contiguous* ranges where both edges move rightward — great for 'longest/shortest substring/subarray satisfying X'. Two pointers converging from opposite ends fits sorted-array problems like Two Sum II or palindrome checks instead.

question: You need many arbitrary range-sum queries on a static (never-changing) array. Sliding Window or Prefix Sum?
choices: Sliding Window — recompute per query
Prefix Sum array — O(n) preprocessing, then O(1) per query
Neither, use a hash map
Segment Tree only
answer: Prefix Sum array — O(n) preprocessing, then O(1) per query
explanation: Sliding window is built for *contiguous, incrementally-moving* windows on data you scan once. For arbitrary range(i,j) queries on unchanging data, a prefix sum array precomputed once answers any query in O(1): sum(i,j) = prefix[j+1]-prefix[i].

question: Your array changes frequently (updates) AND you need range-sum queries repeatedly. Prefix Sum array or Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree)?
choices: Prefix Sum array — O(1) query but O(n) to rebuild after every update
Fenwick Tree — O(log n) update and O(log n) query
Neither supports updates efficiently
Hash Map of running sums
answer: Fenwick Tree — O(log n) update and O(log n) query
explanation: A plain prefix sum array is great for static data but every update forces an O(n) rebuild. A Fenwick Tree (or Segment Tree) supports both point updates and range queries in O(log n), making it the right structure when data is mutable.

question: You need range queries that aren't just sums (e.g. range min/max) on mutable data. Fenwick Tree or Segment Tree?
choices: Fenwick Tree — simplest, but naturally suited to prefix-sum-like (invertible) operations
Segment Tree — more flexible, handles min/max/gcd and other non-invertible operations naturally
Neither can do range min/max
Only a brute-force scan works
answer: Segment Tree — more flexible, handles min/max/gcd and other non-invertible operations naturally
explanation: Fenwick Trees are simpler and faster to code but rely on operations having an inverse (like subtraction for sums). Segment Trees are more general-purpose and directly support range min/max/gcd queries, at the cost of a bit more code and memory.

question: You need to find the next element to the right that's greater than the current one, across a whole array. Nested loops or Monotonic Stack?
choices: Nested loops — O(n²) but simple
Monotonic Stack — O(n), each element pushed/popped once
Sorting the array first
Binary search per element
answer: Monotonic Stack — O(n), each element pushed/popped once
explanation: A monotonic (decreasing) stack processes each element exactly twice (one push, one pop) across the whole array, giving O(n) total — versus O(n²) for checking every pair with nested loops.

question: You need the running median of a growing stream of numbers. Sort on every insert, or Two Heaps?
choices: Re-sort after every insert — O(n log n) per insert
Two Heaps (max-heap for lower half, min-heap for upper half) — O(log n) per insert
A single sorted array with binary insertion — O(n) per insert
Hash Map of counts
answer: Two Heaps (max-heap for lower half, min-heap for upper half) — O(log n) per insert
explanation: Balancing a max-heap (holding the smaller half) against a min-heap (holding the larger half) keeps the median always at the top of one or both heaps, with O(log n) insert instead of O(n log n) re-sorting or O(n) shifting.

question: You need to detect a duplicate/cycle using O(1) extra space (can't use a hash set). Hash Set or Floyd's Fast/Slow Pointers?
choices: Hash Set — O(n) space but simple
Floyd's Fast/Slow Pointers — O(1) space, O(n) time
Both use the same space
Neither can detect cycles
answer: Floyd's Fast/Slow Pointers — O(1) space, O(n) time
explanation: A hash set trades O(n) space for simplicity. When space is constrained, Floyd's tortoise-and-hare (slow moves 1, fast moves 2) detects a cycle in the same O(n) time with only O(1) extra space, by exploiting that a faster pointer must eventually lap a slower one inside a cycle.

question: You need to find the single number that doesn't repeat, where every other number appears exactly twice, using O(1) space. Hash Set or Bit Manipulation (XOR)?
choices: Hash Set — O(n) space to track counts
XOR all numbers together — O(1) space, pairs cancel to zero
Sort first — O(n log n) time
Both are equally good, no real tradeoff
answer: XOR all numbers together — O(1) space, pairs cancel to zero
explanation: XOR-ing the whole array cancels every pair (a^a=0) leaving only the unpaired value, achieving O(n) time with O(1) space — strictly better than a hash set's O(n) space when the input's structure permits it.

question: You need to enumerate all valid combinations/arrangements satisfying constraints (e.g. N-Queens, permutations). Dynamic Programming or Backtracking?
choices: Dynamic Programming — build up all combinations bottom-up
Backtracking — explore choices depth-first, undoing ones that violate constraints
Greedy — pick the best option at each step
BFS level by level
answer: Backtracking — explore choices depth-first, undoing ones that violate constraints
explanation: DP shines when you want an optimal *value* (max/min/count) over overlapping subproblems. When you need to enumerate every valid *configuration* itself (not just count or optimize), backtracking's explore/undo pattern is the natural fit.

question: Multiple threads/processes need concurrent access to a shared queue of tasks. Plain array-based Queue or Circular Buffer?
choices: Plain array-based Queue — dequeuing from the front shifts every remaining element
Circular Buffer (ring buffer) — fixed-size array with wraparound head/tail indices, O(1) enqueue/dequeue
Neither is efficient for queues
A Trie
answer: Circular Buffer (ring buffer) — fixed-size array with wraparound head/tail indices, O(1) enqueue/dequeue
explanation: A naive array queue costs O(n) per dequeue if you shift elements after removing the front. A circular buffer just moves head/tail indices with wraparound, giving true O(1) enqueue/dequeue within a fixed capacity — common in producer/consumer and streaming systems.

question: You need a priority queue backed by an array. Why is a Binary Heap the standard choice over keeping the array sorted?
choices: A sorted array is always faster
A binary heap gives O(log n) insert and O(log n) remove-min/max; a sorted array gives O(n) insert (shifting) despite O(1) remove from one end
They perform identically
A heap requires a linked list, not an array
answer: A binary heap gives O(log n) insert and O(log n) remove-min/max; a sorted array gives O(n) insert (shifting) despite O(1) remove from one end
explanation: Keeping an array sorted makes removing the min/max O(1), but every insertion requires shifting elements to maintain order — O(n). A heap relaxes full ordering (only parent/child ordering matters) so both insert and remove-min/max cost O(log n).

question: You're deduplicating a large list of items where order doesn't matter afterward. Hash Set or a nested loop check against a List?
choices: Nested loop against a growing List — O(n) check per insert, O(n²) total
Hash Set — O(1) average check per insert, O(n) total
Sort the list first, always
Use a Trie for all item types
answer: Hash Set — O(1) average check per insert, O(n) total
explanation: Checking membership in a plain List is O(n) (linear scan), making dedup via nested loops O(n²) overall. A Hash Set's O(1) average membership check brings total dedup time down to O(n).

question: You need ordered iteration (sorted keys) AND O(log n) lookup, insert, and range queries (floor/ceiling). Hash Map or Balanced BST (e.g. TreeMap)?
choices: Hash Map — fastest for everything
Balanced BST (TreeMap/TreeSet) — maintains sorted order with O(log n) operations
Array with binary search — O(n) insert
Linked List
answer: Balanced BST (TreeMap/TreeSet) — maintains sorted order with O(log n) operations
explanation: Hash maps are faster (O(1) average) but give no ordering. When you need sorted iteration or range queries like 'smallest key >= x' (floor/ceiling), a self-balancing BST (Red-Black tree in most standard libraries) is the right tool, trading O(1) for guaranteed O(log n) with order preserved.

question: You need to merge k already-sorted lists/arrays into one sorted output. Concatenate-then-sort, or a Min-Heap based k-way merge?
choices: Concatenate and sort everything — O(N log N) where N is total elements
Min-Heap holding one pointer per list — O(N log k), better when k is small relative to N
Both are always equivalent
Neither approach is standard
answer: Min-Heap holding one pointer per list — O(N log k), better when k is small relative to N
explanation: Ignoring that the lists are already sorted wastes information — concatenate-and-sort is O(N log N). A min-heap of size k (one entry per list) exploits the existing order for O(N log k), which is strictly better whenever k << N.

question: You need substring search (find pattern P in text T) and expect to search the same pattern many times or need guaranteed linear time. Naive scan or KMP?
choices: Naive character-by-character scan — O(n*m) worst case
KMP (Knuth-Morris-Pratt) — O(n+m) worst case using a precomputed failure function
Sort both strings first
Binary search on the text
answer: KMP (Knuth-Morris-Pratt) — O(n+m) worst case using a precomputed failure function
explanation: Naive search can degrade to O(n*m) on adversarial input (e.g. repetitive patterns). KMP precomputes a 'failure function' for the pattern so that on a mismatch, it never re-examines already-matched text characters, guaranteeing O(n+m).

question: Quicksort or Merge Sort: which guarantees O(n log n) worst-case time?
choices: Quicksort — always O(n log n)
Merge Sort — guarantees O(n log n) even in the worst case
Both guarantee the same worst case
Neither guarantees O(n log n)
answer: Merge Sort — guarantees O(n log n) even in the worst case
explanation: Quicksort averages O(n log n) but degrades to O(n²) on adversarial or already-sorted input with a poor pivot choice. Merge Sort always splits evenly, guaranteeing O(n log n), at the cost of O(n) extra space (it's not in-place) — Quicksort is in-place and often faster in practice due to cache locality.

question: You need a stable sort (equal elements keep their relative order), e.g. sorting objects by one field after already sorting by another. Quicksort or Merge Sort?
choices: Quicksort — typically not stable
Merge Sort — naturally stable if implemented carefully
Neither can be made stable
Stability doesn't depend on the algorithm
answer: Merge Sort — naturally stable if implemented carefully
explanation: Merge sort's merge step can preserve the original relative order of equal elements by always taking from the left subarray on ties. Standard in-place quicksort partitioning typically does not preserve this order.

question: You're choosing between BFS and DFS to explore ALL nodes in a graph (not looking for shortest path). Which uses less memory on a wide, shallow graph vs a narrow, deep one?
choices: BFS uses less memory on a wide graph; DFS uses less memory on a deep, narrow graph
BFS always uses less memory
DFS always uses less memory
Memory usage is identical for both
answer: BFS uses less memory on a wide graph; DFS uses less memory on a deep, narrow graph
explanation: BFS's queue holds an entire frontier level, which balloons on wide graphs (many nodes per level). DFS's stack only holds the current path depth, which stays small on deep-but-narrow graphs but can blow up on wide ones if implemented recursively without care.

question: You need to repeatedly build up a large string through many concatenations in a loop. Should you use += in a loop or a mutable buffer (e.g. StringBuilder/list + join)?
choices: String += in a loop is fine, no difference
A mutable buffer (StringBuilder, or list + join) — avoids O(n²) behavior from repeated immutable string copies
Neither matters for performance
Always use recursion instead
answer: A mutable buffer (StringBuilder, or list + join) — avoids O(n²) behavior from repeated immutable string copies
explanation: In languages where strings are immutable, each += creates a brand new string, copying everything so far — O(n) per operation, O(n²) total across n appends. A mutable buffer (StringBuilder, list of parts joined once) amortizes this to O(n) total.

question: A hash map has many keys colliding into the same bucket. Separate Chaining or Open Addressing — which degrades more predictably under high load factor?
choices: Separate Chaining — buckets become linked lists/trees, degrading gracefully to O(k) per bucket
Open Addressing — always stays O(1) no matter the load factor
Both are identical under collisions
Neither approach handles collisions
answer: Separate Chaining — buckets become linked lists/trees, degrading gracefully to O(k) per bucket
explanation: Separate chaining just grows the list (or tree, as Java's HashMap does past a threshold) at the colliding bucket — worst case O(k) for that bucket but the rest of the table is unaffected. Open addressing (linear/quadratic probing) can suffer from clustering and needs careful resizing to avoid severe degradation as load factor approaches 1.

question: An algorithm's runtime doesn't change no matter how large the input gets. What complexity is this?
choices: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)
explanation: Constant time: the number of operations is fixed regardless of input size, e.g. array index access or a hash map lookup.

question: Binary search repeatedly halves the search space. What complexity class does this belong to?
choices: O(n)
O(log n)
O(n log n)
O(sqrt n)
answer: O(log n)
explanation: Each step eliminates half the remaining elements, so the number of steps to shrink n items to 1 is log2(n).

question: Merge sort divides the array in half at each level (log n levels) and does O(n) work merging at each level. What's the total complexity?
choices: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(n²)
O(log n)
answer: O(n log n)
explanation: log n levels of recursion, each doing O(n) total work across that level, multiplies to O(n log n) — the same shape appears in quicksort's average case and any 'divide + linear combine' algorithm.

question: For large enough n, which of these grows fastest?
choices: O(n²)
O(n log n)
O(n!)
answer: O(n!)
explanation: Growth order from slowest to fastest: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2^n) < O(n!). Factorial growth (common in brute-force permutation enumeration) overtakes even exponential growth.

question: A function has a single loop from 0 to n, and inside it calls another function that itself loops from 0 to n. What's the overall time complexity?
choices: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(n²)
O(2n)
answer: O(n²)
explanation: Nested loops each running n times multiply: n iterations × n inner iterations = O(n²), regardless of whether the inner loop is a separate function call.

question: A function halves its input in a loop until it reaches 1, and inside each iteration does an O(n) scan of the original array. What's the total complexity?
choices: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)
O(n²)
answer: O(n log n)
explanation: log n iterations, each doing O(n) work, multiplies to O(n log n) — same pattern as merge sort's combine step.

question: A recursive function calls itself twice on inputs of size n-1 (like naive Fibonacci), with no memoization. What's the time complexity?
choices: O(n)
O(n²)
O(n log n)
explanation: Each call spawns 2 more calls, forming a binary recursion tree of depth n — roughly 2^n total calls without memoization to eliminate the overlapping subproblems.

question: What's the auxiliary space complexity of recursive DFS on a tree of height h, ignoring the input tree itself?
choices: O(h) — the call stack depth
O(n) always
O(n²)
answer: O(h) — the call stack depth
explanation: Auxiliary space counts extra memory beyond the input. Recursive DFS uses stack frames proportional to the deepest path, i.e. the tree's height — O(n) only in the worst case of a completely skewed tree.

question: You can solve Two Sum with O(n²) time and O(1) space (nested loops), or O(n) time and O(n) space (hash map). Which would you pick for a huge array on a memory-constrained device?
choices: Always the O(n) time version — speed matters most
The O(n²) time version — trading time for lower memory usage
It's impossible to make this tradeoff
Rewrite in a different language instead
answer: The O(n²) time version — trading time for lower memory usage
explanation: This is exactly what 'time vs space tradeoff' means: when memory is the binding constraint, accepting slower runtime to avoid extra allocation can be the right engineering call.

question: Appending to a dynamic array (like Python list or Java ArrayList) occasionally triggers an O(n) resize/copy, but individual appends are usually O(1). What's the term for the 'average cost per operation over a sequence'?
choices: Worst-case complexity
Amortized complexity
Best-case complexity
Average-case complexity (different from amortized)
answer: Amortized complexity
explanation: Amortized analysis shows that even though occasional resizes cost O(n), spreading that cost over all the O(1) appends since the last resize gives O(1) amortized per append — a guarantee over any sequence of operations, not just a probabilistic average.

question: You need to compare O(n) vs O(n log n) for n = 1,000,000. Roughly how many times more operations does O(n log n) require?
choices: About 2x
About 20x
About 1,000,000x
They're the same
answer: About 20x
explanation: log2(1,000,000) ≈ 20, so O(n log n) does roughly 20x more work than O(n) at this scale — this is why sorting (n log n) is 'basically linear' in practice for most sizes, while O(n²) at this scale (10^12 ops) would be infeasible.

question: A loop runs i from 1 to n, and inside it, a nested loop runs j from 1 to i (not to n). What's the total complexity?
choices: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(n²)
answer: O(n²)
explanation: The inner loop runs 1+2+3+...+n = n(n+1)/2 times total, which is O(n²) — a triangular loop still simplifies to quadratic, just with a smaller constant factor than a full n×n nested loop.

question: Which sorting algorithm repeatedly finds the minimum remaining element and swaps it into place, using O(1) extra space?
choices: Merge Sort
Selection Sort
Counting Sort
Radix Sort
answer: Selection Sort
explanation: Selection Sort scans the unsorted portion each pass to find the minimum and swaps it to the front — O(n²) time, O(1) space, and NOT stable in its typical swap-based implementation.

question: Which sort builds the sorted array one element at a time by inserting each new element into its correct position among already-sorted elements — efficient on nearly-sorted data?
choices: Bubble Sort
Insertion Sort
Quick Sort
Heap Sort
answer: Insertion Sort
explanation: Insertion Sort is O(n²) worst case but O(n) on already/nearly-sorted input, since few or no shifts are needed — this is why it's often used for small subarrays or as a finishing pass in hybrid sorts like Timsort.

question: You're sorting a list of student records by grade, but want students with the same grade to stay in their original (alphabetical) order. What property must your sort have?
choices: In-place
Stability
O(n log n) worst case
Divide and conquer
answer: Stability
explanation: A stable sort preserves the relative order of equal elements. Merge Sort and Insertion Sort are naturally stable; standard Quick Sort and Heap Sort are not (though stable variants exist with extra bookkeeping).

question: Quick Sort has average O(n log n) time but can degrade to O(n²). When does this worst case happen?
choices: Never, Quick Sort is always O(n log n)
When the pivot repeatedly splits the array very unevenly (e.g. already-sorted input with a naive pivot choice)
When the array has duplicate elements
When the array is very small
answer: When the pivot repeatedly splits the array very unevenly (e.g. already-sorted input with a naive pivot choice)
explanation: If the pivot is always the smallest or largest element (e.g. picking the first element on already-sorted input), each partition only removes one element, giving n levels of O(n) work = O(n²). Randomized or median-of-three pivot selection avoids this in practice.

question: Merge Sort guarantees O(n log n) worst case but uses O(n) extra space. Quick Sort averages O(n log n) with O(log n) space (in-place). When would you prefer Merge Sort?
choices: Never — Quick Sort is strictly better
When you need a stable sort or a guaranteed worst-case bound (e.g. real-time systems), and extra memory is acceptable
When memory is extremely constrained
When the data is already sorted
answer: When you need a stable sort or a guaranteed worst-case bound (e.g. real-time systems), and extra memory is acceptable
explanation: Merge Sort's guaranteed O(n log n) and natural stability make it the right choice for linked lists, external sorting, and systems that can't tolerate Quick Sort's rare O(n²) worst case — Quick Sort tends to win in practice for in-memory arrays due to cache locality and lower constants.

question: You need to sort an array of integers all known to be between 0 and 100. What non-comparison sort achieves O(n+k) time?
choices: Quick Sort
Counting Sort
Merge Sort
Heap Sort
answer: Counting Sort
explanation: Counting Sort counts occurrences of each value (0..k) in O(n+k) time, bypassing the O(n log n) comparison lower bound entirely — but it only works well when the range k is not much larger than n, otherwise the counting array wastes space/time.

question: You need to sort large numbers (e.g. up to 10 digits) without comparing them directly. What sort processes digit by digit?
choices: Radix Sort
Bubble Sort
Selection Sort
Quick Sort
answer: Radix Sort
explanation: Radix Sort sorts by each digit (least or most significant first) using a stable sort like Counting Sort as a subroutine at each digit position, achieving O(nk) for k digits — independent of value magnitude comparisons.

question: Why can't any comparison-based sorting algorithm beat O(n log n) in the worst case?
choices: Hardware limitations
There are n! possible orderings, and a comparison decision tree needs log2(n!) ≈ n log n comparisons to distinguish them all
It's just an empirical observation, not provable
Comparison sorts are always O(n²)
answer: There are n! possible orderings, and a comparison decision tree needs log2(n!) ≈ n log n comparisons to distinguish them all
explanation: This is the information-theoretic lower bound: a binary decision tree of comparisons needs enough depth (leaves = n! outcomes) to distinguish every possible permutation, and log2(n!) is Θ(n log n) by Stirling's approximation.

question: Which of these sorts is NOT in-place (requires O(n) auxiliary space in its standard implementation)?
choices: Quick Sort
Heap Sort
Merge Sort
Insertion Sort
answer: Merge Sort
explanation: Standard Merge Sort allocates a temporary array to merge two sorted halves, costing O(n) extra space. Quick Sort, Heap Sort, and Insertion Sort all sort within the original array using only O(1) or O(log n) extra space.

question: You're sorting a huge dataset that doesn't fit in memory (external sorting from disk). Which sort's divide-and-conquer, sequential-merge structure makes it naturally adaptable to this?
choices: Quick Sort
Merge Sort
Bubble Sort
Selection Sort
answer: Merge Sort
